projects.title: Motoko Language Tooling
projects.summary: A suite of tools that made the Motoko programming language easier to write, test, preview, and embed.
projects.content:
Led development of programming language tooling for Motoko, the smart contract language of the Internet Computer. The tools connect editor workflows with browser and Node.js environments using TypeScript, Rust, and WebAssembly.

- **[VS Code extension](https://github.com/caffeinelabs/vscode-motoko):** type checking, IntelliSense, go to definition, hover docs, import organization, snippets, `dfx.json` validation, one-click temporary deployment, and Mops and Vessel package support. It works standalone without `dfx` on all major operating systems, has more than 85,000 installs, and has had 150+ releases.
- **[Formatter](https://github.com/caffeinelabs/prettier-plugin-motoko) (`prettier-plugin-motoko`, `mo-fmt`):** a Prettier plugin and standalone CLI with import organization, used by 550+ projects.
- **[Live-reload server](https://github.com/caffeinelabs/motoko-dev-server) (`mo-dev`, `mo-test`):** redeploys canisters, regenerates type declarations, and runs `*.test.mo` unit tests on file change; used by 400+ projects.
- **[Compiler npm package](https://github.com/caffeinelabs/node-motoko) (`motoko`):** compiles and runs Motoko in Node.js or the browser, with a virtual file system, Candid and WebAssembly output, parse trees, and GitHub package loading; used by 460+ projects.
- **[Embed service](https://github.com/caffeinelabs/embed-motoko) ([announcement](https://levelup.gitconnected.com/embed-motoko-interactive-smart-contracts-in-your-medium-story-or-blog-post-58c85719eee6)):** interactive, runnable Motoko snippets for Medium articles, blogs, and websites via iframe and oEmbed.
- **[Starter projects](https://github.com/rvanasa/vite-react-motoko):** Vite + React + Motoko template (58 stars, 30+ forks), plus [Motoko + Rust](https://github.com/rvanasa/motoko-rust-starter), [Vite + React + Rust](https://github.com/rvanasa/vite-react-icp-rust), and [Advent of Code](https://github.com/rvanasa/aoc-motoko-starter) templates.
- **Language and library utilities:** [`mo-convert`](https://github.com/rvanasa/mo-convert) (90+ consistently named base library type conversions), syntax highlighting for [highlight.js](https://github.com/rvanasa/highlightjs-motoko) and the [Discourse](https://github.com/rvanasa/discourse-highlightjs-motoko) developer forum.

projects.title: Blocks
projects.summary: A low-code, drag-and-drop smart contract editor, funded by a $25,000 DFINITY Developer Grant.
projects.content:
Blocks is an online visual smart contract builder for the Internet Computer blockchain. Inspired by node-based editors such as Blender Nodes and Unreal Engine Blueprint, it lets developers build Motoko smart contracts by connecting blocks in a dataflow graph, then compile, deploy, and test them directly from the browser.

Built with React and JavaScript with a collaborator, and funded by a $25,000 DFINITY Developer Grant. Features include interactive tutorials, example and template contracts (such as fungible tokens and DIP721 NFTs), pretty-printed Motoko output, custom expression blocks that mix visual logic with Motoko syntax, GitHub package imports, built-in test cases, and an embeddable `react-blocks-editor` npm package. The repository has 160+ GitHub stars.

[Web application](https://blocks-editor.github.io/blocks/) · [Homepage](https://blocks-editor.github.io/) · [Source code](https://github.com/Blocks-Editor/blocks) · [Design process](https://levelup.gitconnected.com/how-we-created-blocks-an-online-drag-and-drop-smart-contract-editor-fe23eff4d933)

projects.title: Incremental Computation Visualizer
projects.summary: An online visualization tool for the paper 'Fungi: Typed incremental computation with names.'
projects.content:
Built an interactive visualization tool in Rust to accompany research on typed incremental computation with names. The project made the programming language output explorable in a browser.

Incremental computations reuse work that is unaffected when their inputs change. To do this in a general-purpose language, programmers need a way to identify which dynamic allocations (data and subcomputations) correspond across runs. Fungi, a typed functional language by Matthew A. Hammer, Jana Dunfield, Kyle Headley, Monal Narasimhamurthy, and Dimitrios J. Economou, makes these names formal and statically verifiable. Its type-and-effect system lets programmers encode local invariants about names and use them to prove global uniqueness, meaning names are used correctly. The paper proves that well-typed Fungi programs respect global uniqueness, and a Rust prototype of the language was applied to a library of incremental collections.

The visualizer lets readers step through Fungi programs and inspect their incremental behavior directly in the browser, instead of reading only the formal semantics.

[Paper on arXiv](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.07826)

The interface supports stacked parameter panels (for example 500 mb heights alongside surface vorticity and 0-3 km MLCAPE), time navigation, and regional sectors.

A major update in April 2026 ([announcement](https://x.com/rvandersmith/status/2041603976441856365)) added:

- Dark mode
- All SPC mesoanalysis products
- WPC surface analysis
- Pivotal Weather model data
- Point soundings
- Shareable URLs for real-time and archived data

projects.title: Stepwise CAPE/CIN
projects.summary: Designed and contributed an inflow layer visualization to the SounderPy sounding plot package.
projects.content:
Designed and contributed a stepwise CAPE/CIN inflow layer visualization to [SounderPy](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy), a Python package used to generate sounding plots for meteorology research papers. The visualization helps determine whether an environment is likely to produce surface-based or elevated thunderstorms.

## Motivation

Soundings are usually summarized with single values such as SBCAPE and MUCAPE, which can hide where a storm's inflow actually comes from. I proposed [showing CAPE and CIN at every level of the atmosphere](https://bsky.app/profile/ryanvandersmith.com/post/3ldkhf2f5fs2u) so that tornadic, "mothership," and large-hail environments can be recognized at a glance.

The plot is a way to visualize the effective inflow layer (EIL), the lowest contiguous layer of air that can feed a storm's updraft. Operational tools approximate it with a single layer, which can be misleading in elevated environments where inflow comes from one or more layers above the surface.

## What it shows

- **Surface-based and tornadic:** a thick layer of uninhibited inflow near the surface, such as the 0-2 km layer in the 2024 Greenfield tornado environment, which is highly favorable for tornadoes.
- **Elevated:** inflow comes from layers above the surface, as in a sounding that produced 2.5" hail. Small amounts of CAPE can even exist above 6 km.
- **Large CAPE with large surface CIN:** often associated with photogenic, laminar "mothership" supercells. The stable air tends to keep tornadoes from forming, and these storms often start elevated before tapping lower-level CAPE.

## Pull requests

### Original inflow plot

[Pull request #33](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/33) added an opt-in `show_inflow` option to `build_sounding()`, drawing CAPE, 3CAPE, and CIN at each level on the skew-T. It added about 1-2% to the runtime of `build_sounding()`.

2023 Akron, CO supercell, which produced 27 tornadoes:

![Inflow plot for the 2023 Akron, CO supercell](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/afebaac9-c004-4332-a643-7e5c0407e9dc)

2024 messy MCS and tornado bust near Lufkin, TX, with a secondary inflow layer from 700-500 mb:

![Inflow plot near Lufkin, TX](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c4435c09-c6ba-4d2f-b780-8ddf79552945)

2024 Shreveport, LA tornado associated with Hurricane Beryl:

![Inflow plot for the Shreveport, LA tornado](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/882bdad0-7550-4a62-9d4e-a024bd7dfb43)

2024 Bedford, TX 2" hail event (elevated inflow):

![Inflow plot for the Bedford, TX hail event](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/dc14e116-ef0d-4e18-a528-b3b8ec4f4f7f)

### Merged version

SounderPy's maintainer, Kyle Gillett, suggested moving the visualization into the 0-3 km vertical plots at the bottom right of the sounding, next to the kinematics, to show what a storm is actually "feeling." [Pull request #34](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/34) replaced the "Theta & Theta-e" plot with "CIN & 3CAPE" and kept the original plot available behind a `show_theta` flag for backwards compatibility.

Compared with #33, it reduces information overload on the skew-T and is better for low-level storm behavior, at the cost of no longer showing mid- and upper-level convection.

Tornadic supercells:

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for tornadic supercells](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ee08e0be-4393-4ff1-94cd-f0f1f02276bc)

Elevated supercells:

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for elevated supercells](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/24d8e3ba-548a-4319-ae91-fea27a7b7608)

In-between cases (almost or slightly surface-based):

![CIN and 3CAPE plot for in-between cases](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c8584225-d12d-4c3e-84cb-4efd45d7374f)

Kyle then refined the design with fixed axis limits (CIN down to -300 J/kg, CAPE up to 2100 J/kg) and plotted CAPE instead of 3CAPE, so that soundings can be compared directly. Because anything above about 2000 J/kg indicates severity rather than inflow structure, this range works as a cutoff. The reworked version was merged in [pull request #35](https://github.com/kylejgillett/sounderpy/pull/35).

![Final plot with fixed CIN and CAPE axis limits](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/547f701b-a2da-4146-b00e-f698f7f6e747)

## Links

- [Bluesky thread with examples](https://bsky.app/profile/ryanvandersmith.com/post/3ldkhf2f5fs2u)
- [Effective inflow layer research (Monthly Weather Review)](https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/mwre/148/8/mwrD200013.xml)

projects.title: Cloud Inversion Forecast
projects.summary: A model-driven fog and cloud inversion forecast tool used by photographers in Colorado.
projects.content:
Built a forecast app that combines high-resolution model output (HRRR, RAP, NAMNest) to predict fog, low clouds, and cloud inversions at selected viewpoints. It spread by word of mouth among Colorado photographers and is also used for my own weather photography.

A cloud inversion happens when temperature increases with height near the surface instead of decreasing. Cold, dense air pools in valleys beneath a warmer layer, and the warm layer acts as a lid. Moisture trapped below condenses into fog or low cloud, leaving mountain peaks above a "sea of clouds". Forecasting one means finding the inversion layer and checking that its height, humidity, and wind line up with the terrain.

[Beautiful and Devastating Temperature Inversions, Explained](https://ryanvandersmith.medium.com/beautiful-and-devastating-temperature-inversions-explained-10cb489dc46e)

profile.name: Ryan Vandersmith
profile.tagline: R&D software engineer building forecasting, visualization, and analysis tools for meteorology and atmospheric science.
profile.summary: Ryan Vandersmith is an R&D software engineer with over 10 years of experience and a deep self-taught background in meteorology. He builds weather forecasting and analysis tools used by photographers, storm chasers, and researchers, including Mesoview (skychaser.mesoview.app), a cloud inversion forecast tool, a mountain wave visualization tool, and a stepwise CAPE/CIN contribution to SounderPy. Professionally, he worked on Caffeine.ai, an AI website builder, and led Motoko programming-language tooling, including a VS Code extension with more than 85,000 installs. He also has experience with cross-chain EVM integrations, developer-experience products, UX research, Rust research software at the University of Colorado Boulder, consulting, and public-sector software.
expertise: weather forecasting and atmospheric analysis tools
